summary: Ronald and Nancy Reagan, despite many gay friends from their Hollywood years, led a US administration that ignored, mocked and underfunded the response to AIDS through the 1980s as tens of thousands died, while Surgeon General C. Everett Koop pushed back.

evidence.note: 1960s: Reagans groomed for politics, Nancy's gay designer and socialite friends; start of covered span
1967 governorship; gay aides exposed and fired
1978 Briggs Initiative and Reagan's opposition to it
1982 press briefing where the press secretary and reporters joke about AIDS
1980 campaign: evangelical group's anti-gay ads helped Reagan carry the South
1985: Hudson collapses in Paris; Nancy declines to help his transfer to a French military hospital
1985: Reagan first says the word AIDS in public after Hudson's announcement
Defence of Reagan's FDA reforms weighed against cuts and industry-friendly deregulation
Koop's background as evangelical pediatric surgeon and his contested appointment
1986 Koop report calls for school sex education; backlash and Bauer's rival education policy
Reagan leaves office in 1989; later death tolls and the 2013 claim are short codas

notes: Partial life: the story is framed around the Reagans' AIDS response; their earlier lives get only Hollywood-era and governorship background, so covered_span starts in the early 1960s (approximate, 'Kennedy years'). Roles are a loose fit: politician-official covers Nancy as first lady; entertainer-artist reflects the Hollywood-friends segment. FR is brief (Hudson in Paris).
